intro: Martha Argerich plays Prokofiev’s Toccata in D minor, Op. 11, which opens with a single repeated D passed between the hands and closes with the D played across the whole keyboard. Between the opening and the close, chromatic lines move beneath the repeated notes.

sections.label: A · Repeated D shared between the hands
sections.mNote: Repeated notes widen into chromatic lines.

sections.label: A′ · Repeated-note figure, reprise
sections.mNote: The opening figure returns, then the hands move apart.

sections.label: Dev · Triads against chromatic lines
sections.mNote: The hands descend at different times, then climb apart.

sections.label: A″ · Repeated D returns in octaves
sections.mNote: Both hands play the repeated note in octaves.

sections.label: Coda · Glissando and two Ds
sections.mNote: A final ascent reaches both ends of the keyboard

cues.title: Opening, repeated Ds
cues.text: The hands take turns striking D, the left an octave below the right, in continuous semiquavers. The left hand then moves up and down in semitones while the right outlines a chord of D minor.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, Op. 11, opening. The written sequence of repeated Ds, chromatic left-hand patterns and D-minor triad is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Derzhanovsky, April 1912
cues.text: On 24 April 1912 Nikolay Myaskovsky wrote to the critic Vladimir Derzhanovsky about the new Toccata. He praised its simple themes and added: “I can’t help but scream in delight.”
cues.evidence: Myaskovsky to Derzhanovsky, 11/24 April 1912, quoted in Simon Morrison’s Henle HN 1581 preface (2023), pp. IV–V, from Iosif Kunin’s collection of Myaskovsky documents (1981), p. 43. https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: Return of the repeated-note theme
cues.text: After the chromatic lines have spread across the keyboard, the opening repeated-note figure returns. Prokofiev augments its rhythm and follows it with a short pause. The hands then move apart again.
cues.evidence: The Toccata’s first return of the repeated-note theme is followed by rhythmic augmentation, a short pause and independently descending triad figures. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Brooklyn Museum recital, 1918
cues.text: At the Brooklyn Museum on 29 October 1918, Prokofiev played before a reception for Boris Anisfeld’s paintings and theatre designs. He softened the Toccata for the guests and left out notes. The unsigned review in the next day’s Brooklyn Daily Eagle compared him to a lion roaring like a dove.
cues.evidence: Simon Morrison, Henle HN 1581 preface, p. V, citing the unsigned Brooklyn Daily Eagle review, 30 October 1918, p. 7. The image of lion and dove is paraphrased. https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: Return of the repeated-note theme
cues.text: The opening D returns in alternating octaves, now in both hands. It comes back after chromatic scales and clashing chords, and this time it covers much more of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, final return of the repeated-note theme; alternating D octaves in both hands. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars
cues.text: The music slows and stops, then the piano climbs once more in chromatic steps. An upward glissando leads to the final chord, two D octaves marked sforzando at opposite ends of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, closing passage: slowdown, pause, chromatic ascent, glissando and final sforzando D octaves. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Return of the repeated-note figure
transitions.from: A · Repeated D shared between the hands
transitions.how: The chromatic thirds lead back to the repeated-note figure. The writing thins and the rhythm broadens, and a pause comes before the next passage. In that passage both hands play triad figures and descend at different times.
transitions.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, first return of the repeated-note theme and following triad passage. The score’s sequence is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev).

transitions.title: Chromatic lines converge on D
transitions.to: A″ · Repeated D returns in octaves
transitions.how: Minor triads climb in the right hand while chromatic octaves descend in the left. The descending-thirds tune returns around D, then both hands take up repeated D octaves. The single repeated notes of the opening are now octaves played by both hands.
transitions.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata: contrary-motion chromatic writing, descending-thirds theme in D and the return of repeated D octaves. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)

transitions.title: Slowdown, pause and chromatic ascent
transitions.from: A″ · Repeated D returns in octaves
transitions.how: The repeated octaves slow down and stop. When the notes return, they rise as a chromatic scale. Octave chords and an upward glissando follow. Prokofiev ends the piece with two accented D octaves, one at each end of the keyboard.
transitions.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, final passage: slowdown and pause, chromatic ascent, glissando and two sforzando D octaves. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)

composer.born: 27 April (15 April Old Style) 1891; Prokofiev himself gave 23 April, Sontsovka, Ukraine, then Russian Empire
composer.epithet: Twentieth-century composer known for Romeo and Juliet, with its writing for strings, and for his piano music.
facts: Glière at Sontsovka, 1902–03; St Petersburg Conservatory, 1904–14
Russia · United States · Bavaria · Paris; settled in Moscow in 1936
The Love for Three Oranges · Romeo and Juliet · Cinderella · War and Peace
Seven symphonies, five piano concertos and nine completed piano sonatas

quote.text: It seemed to me that if Haydn had lived into our own time, he would have kept his way of writing while taking in something new.
quote.source: Prokofiev, short Autobiography (1941), recalling the summer of 1917; our translation

composer.background:
At Sontsovka, the Ukrainian estate his father managed, Prokofiev grew up hearing his mother play Beethoven and Chopin. She wrote down his first piano pieces; the earliest, an Indian Galop, dates from 1896. After a trip to the Moscow opera in 1900, the eight-year-old set about writing an opera of his own, The Giant, for the family to perform at home. His mother eventually stopped playing when she saw that he had overtaken her. Sergei Taneyev recommended proper lessons, and Reinhold Glière spent the summers of 1902 and 1903 at Sontsovka teaching the boy, who was already filling manuscript books.

He entered the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen, bringing four operas, two sonatas, a symphony and piano pieces to the entrance examination. Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration, Lyadov harmony and counterpoint; later Anna Esipova took charge of his piano playing. Nikolai Tcherepnin taught conducting and encouraged his taste for Haydn and Mozart. His fellow student Nikolai Myaskovsky became the friend to whom he sent scores and complaints for the rest of his life. In December 1908 Prokofiev played some of his first distinctive pieces, Suggestion diabolique among them, at St Petersburg’s Evenings of Contemporary Music. The following spring his examination pieces shocked Lyadov, who heard Scriabin in them. In the final piano competition of 1914, with Esipova ill, Prokofiev played his own First Concerto. Glazunov opposed him, but Prokofiev was awarded the Rubinstein Prize, which was a grand piano.
